paras: The killing of Albert West was the fatal shooting of a young Black prisoner by a guard at the Indianapolis work-house on March 2, 1888. The guard, Stewart, said West had attacked him with stones and fractured his skull before he fired, and that version, drawn from his own ante-mortem statement, was the only one the papers printed. The Indianapolis Journal gave the case a long local account, while a short wire dispatch carried it to papers from Kansas to New York and weekly digests repeated it through March.

West had been sent to the work-house on December 30 for thirty days and a $25 fine after cutting his step-father, Wm. West, about the head during a quarrel over a young woman he brought to the house. According to the Journal, the mayor thought he should have been charged with assault with intent to kill, and the step-father had asked only days earlier how to protect himself once Albert was released. With about a week left to serve, West was described by work-house officers as a troublesome prisoner who especially resisted breaking stone.

On the morning of March 2, guard Ananias Stewart ordered West, at work on the stone-pile, to break up stone left by the afternoon gang; West refused and threatened the guard with his hammer when told he would go to the dungeon. In the Journal's account, West walked quietly beside the guard for a distance, then broke away toward the gate, where Stewart caught him and West grappled for the guard's Winchester rifle. After Stewart regained the rifle, West threw pieces of stone, two of which struck the guard's head, cutting the temporal artery and fracturing the skull, and Stewart then shot him in the left side below the shoulder. West died within a few minutes, and Stewart collapsed unconscious.

Coroner Wagner and Dr. Brennan revived the guard enough to take an ante-mortem statement, which the Journal said was the source of its account. Stewart's condition was called dangerous but not hopeless, and he was taken to his home in North Indianapolis. The coroner made a post-mortem examination of West's body, which was then sent to his step-father's home; no coroner's verdict, arrest or later report on the guard's recovery appears in the coverage.

The Indianapolis Journal headlined the story 'A Young Desperado Killed' and described West as 'a Negro Work-House Prisoner' who 'Murderously Assaults a Guard', opening with a long paragraph on his violence toward his family. The wire dispatch dated Indianapolis, March 2, ran the next day in the Wichita Eagle as 'Killed Instantly' and in the New York Sun as 'An Eaeaplnc [Escaping] Prisoner Snot [Shot] Dead', and on March 8 in the Emporia Weekly News as 'Killed For Assaulting his Guard'. Weekly digests compressed it to one sentence: the Indiana State Sentinel called West 'a colored tough', the National Tribune listed it among 'Crimes and Casualties', and a 'South and West' column in the Narragansett Herald and the Abbeville Press and Banner said he had crushed a prison official's head with a stone. No version quoted any witness other than the guard.

The wire named the guard James Stewart and said a revolver bullet struck West's heart as he tried to escape, while the local paper, which reported the post-mortem, named him Ananias and described a Winchester ball in the left side after West had been caught. The Indiana State Sentinel placed the shooting on 'last Monday', against the Friday, March 2, date of the wire and the Journal.

reader.title: Killing of Albert West
bases: A workhouse guard shot and killed a prisoner in his charge; no mob or crowd took part (A1, A2, A4).

The local Indianapolis Journal (A1), the March 2 wire dispatch (A2) and the Indiana State Sentinel (A4) agree that guard Stewart shot West dead at the workhouse after West attacked him, though the account of the assault rests on the guard's own statement (A1).

accounts.gist: West refused to break stone, was being led to the dungeon, broke away toward the gate, grappled for the guard's Winchester, then threw stones that fractured the guard's skull; Stewart then shot him in the left side.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: West attacked guard Stewart with a stone, crushing his skull; though badly hurt, Stewart fired as West tried to escape and a revolver bullet hit West's heart.

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Journal headlined 'A Young Desperado Killed' and devoted its opening paragraph to West's record of violence at home.
Out-of-state papers ran the brief March 2 dispatch under headlines such as 'Killed Instantly' and 'Killed For Assaulting his Guard'.
Weekly digests reduced it to a sentence, the State Sentinel calling West 'a colored tough'.

info: Morning of Friday, March 2, 1888, per the wire dispatch and the local paper ('yesterday' in its March 3 issue); the Indiana State Sentinel said 'last Monday'.
Stone-pile of the Indianapolis work-house ('the stone house'), near its gate.
Albert West (headline of the local paper prints 'Alfred'), described as 'a young colored man' and 'a Negro Work-House Prisoner'.

Serving a workhouse sentence of thirty days and a $25 fine for assault on his step-father, Wm. West (the wire says 'his father'); on the day, accused by the guard of refusing to break stone, fleeing, and striking the guard with stones.
Workhouse guard Stewart, named Ananias Stewart in the local paper and 'Nanias' in one wire reprint, James Stewart in another.
West's body went to Ripley & Hedges's undertaking establishment and then to his step-father's home; no arrest or charge of the guard was reported.
